meaning: A strong, old-fashioned prohibition: “must not ...”. 「べからざる」 modifies a noun: “that must not / cannot be ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べからず / べからざる + noun (する → するべからず / すべからず)

senses.label: Must not (prohibition)
senses.meaning: A strong ban, like “No ...!” or “Thou shalt not ...”. It sounds stiff and archaic. You see it on signs, slogans and in proverbs. In speech, people only use it jokingly.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べからず. Common: 「立ち入るべからず」, 「入るべからず」, 「忘るべからず」
examples: No entry except for authorized personnel.
Keep off the grass.
Never forget your original resolve.

senses.label: That cannot be ...
senses.meaning: 「べからざる」 + noun means “that must not / cannot be ...”. It forms set phrases like 「欠くべからざる」 (“indispensable”). Written style.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べからざる + noun. Common: 「欠くべからざる」, 「許すべからざる」, 「侵すべからざる」
examples: Water is indispensable to daily life.
That is an unforgivable act.
He is indispensable to this team.

notes: For 「する」, you can say 「するべからず」 or the more classical 「すべからず」.
「すべからく」 is an adverb meaning “by rights, all”. It is unrelated to this pattern.
「べからず」 is only for signs and proverbs. For everyday prohibitions, use 「〜てはいけない」 or 「〜ないでください」.

daily.title: Reading a sign
daily.description: A prohibition sign at a temple or a construction site.
daily.example: No entry beyond this point.

daily.title: Hearing a proverb
daily.description: An older person quotes an old saying to teach a young one.
daily.example: He who does not work shall not eat, you know.

daily.title: Joking around
daily.description: A note on the fridge, written in a mock-stern tone.
daily.example: This pudding: thou shalt not eat.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: A formal document listing prohibited actions.
work.example: Confidential company materials must not be taken off the premises.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: An editorial stresses how important something is.
work.example: Trust is an indispensable asset for a company.

etymology: From 「べから」, the irrealis form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」, plus the negative auxiliary 「ず」. 「ざる」 is the attributive form of 「ず」, so it can modify nouns.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: 「べきではない」 is modern Japanese for “should not”, a piece of advice. 「べからず」 is an archaic, strong prohibition used on signs.

similar.title: 〜な (prohibition)
similar.explanation: 「な」 is a spoken, direct command to a person: “Don't!”. 「べからず」 is a written notice not aimed at anyone in particular.

similar.title: 〜まじき
similar.explanation: 「まじき」 means “unbecoming of (one's position)” and carries blame. 「べからざる」 focuses on “cannot / must not”.

similar.title: 〜てはならない
similar.explanation: 「てはならない」 is a modern written prohibition used in rules and lectures. 「べからず」 is older and sounds like a slogan.

meaning: Written style. Expresses purpose, “in order to ...”, with strong determination.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べく (する → するべく / すべく)

senses.label: In order to ...
senses.meaning: Someone does the second action to achieve a goal. It sounds formal and stiff. Common in news, official documents and speeches. The second clause cannot be a command or request.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べく, ... Common: 「〜を実現すべく」, 「〜を解明すべく」, 「〜になるべく」
examples: I keep working hard every day to make my dream come true.
An investigation is underway to find the cause of the accident.
He studied like crazy in order to become a doctor.

notes: The second clause cannot be a command, request or invitation: ✕「合格すべく勉強しなさい」.
The adverb 「なるべく」 (“as much as possible”) is unrelated.
「〜べくもない」 (“there is no way ...”) and 「〜べくして」 (“inevitably ...”) are separate patterns.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on a rescue operation.
daily.example: An all-out search continues to rescue the missing people.

daily.title: Reading a biography
daily.description: A biography describes the hero's resolve.
daily.example: He left his hometown to support his family.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: Explaining to customers why a service changed.
work.example: We have overhauled our system in order to improve service quality.

work.title: Project report
work.description: A report explains why a team was formed.
work.example: A dedicated team was formed to open up new markets.

etymology: From 「べく」, the continuative form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 「べし」 expresses obligation or intention. Linked to a following clause, it came to mean “intending to ... (and so)”, that is, purpose.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 「ために」 is the all-purpose expression, fine in speech and writing. 「べく」 is written style and shows stronger will.

similar.title: 〜んがため（に）
similar.explanation: Both are very formal. 「んがため」 is stronger and more dramatic, with a feeling of “no matter what”.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: 「ように」 usually follows non-volitional verbs or potential forms. 「べく」 follows volitional verbs.

similar.title: 〜べくもない
similar.explanation: 「べくもない」 means “there is no way ...”. It has nothing to do with purpose 「べく」.

meaning: Written style. “Unbecoming of (a ...), that should never be done”, with strong condemnation.
connection: Verb dictionary form + まじき + noun (する → するまじき / すまじき); often noun + に (として) あるまじき

senses.label: Unbecoming of one's position
senses.meaning: 「〜にあるまじき」 means something does not fit a certain position or role. It is used to condemn someone's words or actions. Often with 「行為」, 「発言」, 「態度」.
senses.connection: Noun (教師, 政治家, 社会人, etc.) + に / として + あるまじき + noun
examples: Using violence against students is conduct unbecoming of a teacher.
That remark is unacceptable for a politician.

senses.label: That should never be ...
senses.meaning: Placed directly after a verb: “that must never be ...”. Very strong, stronger than 「べきではない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + まじき + noun. Common: 「許すまじき」, 「言うまじき」
examples: That is a crime that must never be forgiven.
I said something that should never be said in front of children.

notes: It only modifies nouns. It cannot end a sentence.
Mainly used to criticize others. When used about yourself, it shows deep regret.
The slang 「マジ」 in 「マジきつい」 (“seriously tough”) is unrelated.

daily.title: Social news
daily.description: A news report on police misconduct.
daily.example: It is a scandal unworthy of police officers, who are supposed to protect citizens.

daily.title: Chatting with a friend
daily.description: A friend talks about a celebrity's gaffe.
daily.example: That's no way for an adult to behave, right?

work.title: Disciplinary notice
work.description: HR explains the penalty for an employee who broke the rules.
work.example: This incident was conduct unbecoming of an employee and will be dealt with strictly.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: Commenting on an official's wrongdoing.
work.example: Misconduct unworthy of a civil servant has come to light.

etymology: 「まじき」 is the attributive form of the classical negative conjectural auxiliary 「まじ」. 「まじ」 is the negative counterpart of 「べし」, meaning “should not, will not”.

similar.title: 〜べからざる
similar.explanation: 「べからざる」 focuses on “cannot, must not”, as in 「欠くべからざる」. 「まじき」 focuses on “unbecoming of one's position” and carries strong blame.

similar.title: 〜べきではない
similar.explanation: 「べきではない」 is general advice and can end a sentence. 「まじき」 only modifies nouns and is much stronger.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: 「まい」 expresses negative guesses or negative will. 「まじき」 means “that should not be”. They are related in origin but used differently.

meaning: Shows resolve, “if worst comes to worst, I'll just ...”, or explains oneself, “I merely ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ta-form + までだ / までのことだ

senses.label: I'll just ... then
senses.meaning: If the first option fails, you will simply do this instead, and that's no big deal. It shows a “so what” determination. Often paired with 「〜なら」, 「〜ても」, 「〜ば」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + までだ / までのことだ. Common: 「〜ならば、〜までだ」
examples: If there are no trains, I'll just walk home.
If I fail, I'll simply start over.
If it really doesn't work, I'll just give up.

senses.label: I merely ...
senses.meaning: You only did something, with no other intention. Used to explain or justify yourself in a low-key way.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + までだ / までのことだ. Common: 「〜たまでだ」, 「〜たまでのことです」
examples: I was only telling the truth.
I was just asking, that's all.
I was merely following the rules.

notes: After the dictionary form it means “I'll just ...”; after the ta-form it means “I merely ...”. The meanings differ.
「〜ばそれまでだ」 (“once ..., it's all over”) is a different pattern.
The 「まで」 of time limits, as in 「五時までだ」, is unrelated.

daily.title: Asked about your plans
daily.description: A friend worries you won't get a ticket.
daily.example: If I can't get a ticket, I'll just watch the stream at home.

daily.title: When misunderstood
daily.description: Someone thinks you were being sarcastic, so you explain.
daily.example: I wasn't being sarcastic. I just said what I thought.

daily.title: Talking about exams
daily.description: Showing you aren't afraid of failing.
daily.example: If I fail this year, I'll simply take it again next year.

work.title: Negotiating with a client
work.description: Stating your position when the other side rejects your terms.
work.example: If the terms don't work, we'll simply look for another business partner.

work.title: Praised by your boss
work.description: Replying modestly.
work.example: Not at all. I only did what a manager should do.

etymology: The particle 「まで」 marks the end point or limit of a range. “Up to this point and no further” came to mean “that's all there is to it” or “going this far is enough”.

similar.title: 〜ばそれまでだ
similar.explanation: 「ばそれまでだ」 means “once ..., it's all over”. 「までだ」 means “I'll just ..., that's all”.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: 「にすぎない」 objectively says “it's nothing more than ...”. 「たまでだ」 is the speaker justifying their own action.

similar.title: 〜ほかない
similar.explanation: 「ほかない」 means “have no choice but to ...”, with resignation. 「までだ」 has a carefree “so what” resolve.

meaning: Covered with dirt or liquid on the surface; figuratively, mired in something bad.
connection: Noun + まみれ (だ / の + noun / になる)

senses.label: Covered in (literal)
senses.meaning: The whole body or a surface is covered in mud, blood, sweat, dust, etc. Usually something unpleasant, giving a sense of being a mess.
senses.connection: Noun (泥, 汗, 血, ほこり, 油, etc.) + まみれ. Common: 「泥まみれになる」, 「汗まみれの〜」
examples: The children were playing and got covered in mud.
I washed my sweat-soaked shirt.
A dust-covered book turned up in the storeroom.

senses.label: Mired in (figurative)
senses.meaning: Someone or something is full of negative things, such as debt, scandal or lies.
senses.connection: Noun (借金, 疑惑, 嘘, etc.) + まみれ
examples: He is living a life buried in debt.
That politician is riddled with suspicion.

notes: 「まみれ」 stresses liquids or powders sticking to a surface. You can't say ✕「傷まみれ」; say 「傷だらけ」.
It is almost always used for negative things.
The verb form is 「まみれる」, as in 「血にまみれた手」.

daily.title: Kids come home from playing
daily.description: A mother sees the state of her child.
daily.example: What happened? You're covered in mud!

daily.title: After exercise
daily.description: Complaining to a friend after a run.
daily.example: By the time I finished running, I was drenched in sweat.

daily.title: Spring cleaning
daily.description: Cleaning a room that hasn't been used in ages.
daily.example: The air-conditioner filter was caked with dust.

work.title: Factory work
work.description: Describing mechanics' working conditions.
work.example: The mechanics are working covered in grease.

work.title: Business news
work.description: A report on a company's worsening finances.
work.example: That company is drowning in debt and on the verge of bankruptcy.

etymology: From the continuative form of the verb 「まみれる（塗れる）」, “to be smeared with, to be covered in”. Usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜だらけ
similar.explanation: 「だらけ」 means “full of, all over”, in large numbers, as in 「傷だらけ」 or 「間違いだらけ」. 「まみれ」 stresses liquids or powders coating a surface.

similar.title: 〜ずくめ
similar.explanation: 「ずくめ」 means “nothing but ...” and can be positive, as in 「いいことずくめ」. 「まみれ」 is only for bad things.

similar.title: 〜ぐるみ
similar.explanation: 「ぐるみ」 means “including ..., as a whole”, as in 「家族ぐるみ」. It has no sense of being dirty.

meaning: Follows a noun: “to have a touch of ..., to seem somewhat like ...”.
connection: Noun + めく / めいて / めいた + noun

senses.label: A touch of ...
senses.meaning: Usually with seasons: the feel of that season is gradually arriving. Often with 「〜てきた」. It sounds elegant and lyrical.
senses.connection: 春, 秋, 夏, etc. + めく. Common: 「春めいてきた」, 「秋めいた風」
examples: The sunlight has become quite spring-like.
Mornings and evenings feel quite autumnal now, don't they?

senses.label: Sort of like ...
senses.meaning: Not exactly the thing, but with that flavor or appearance. Usually 「〜めいた + noun」. Often slightly negative or subtle.
senses.connection: Noun (皮肉, 謎, 冗談, 言い訳, 説教, etc.) + めいた + noun / めいて
examples: He spoke in a somewhat sarcastic tone.
She gave a mysterious smile.
I don't want to say anything that sounds like an excuse.

senses.label: Pretending to be ...
senses.meaning: The transitive form 「〜めかす」 means to deliberately give that appearance. The most common is 「冗談めかして」, “half-jokingly”.
senses.connection: Noun + めかす / めかして. Common: 「冗談めかして」
examples: He half-jokingly said what he really thought.

notes: 「めく」 is a godan verb. Before nouns, 「めいた」 is more common than 「めく」.
Words like 「ときめく」, 「ざわめく」 and 「きらめく」 are independent words, not this pattern.
Only certain nouns can take it, so learn it as set combinations.

daily.title: Seasonal greetings
daily.description: Chatting about the weather with a neighbor.
daily.example: It's really starting to feel like spring, isn't it?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a mysterious character.
daily.example: The man left a cryptic remark and went away.

daily.title: Chatting with friends
daily.description: Talking about something a friend said as a joke.
daily.example: He said it half-jokingly, but I think he meant it.

work.title: Seasonal letter
work.description: The seasonal greeting at the start of a business letter.
work.example: Autumn is deepening day by day. We hope this finds you well.

work.title: Meeting feedback
work.description: Describing a boss's talk that felt like a lecture.
work.example: The department manager's preachy talk went on for a full thirty minutes.

etymology: 「めく」 is an old suffix that attaches to nouns and other words to form verbs meaning “to show signs of ...”. Words like 「ときめく」 and 「きらめく」 also come from it.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「っぽい」 is colloquial and very flexible. It can also show tendencies (「忘れっぽい」). 「めく」 is more literary and works with fewer words.

similar.title: 〜じみる
similar.explanation: 「じみる」 is usually negative, as in 「年寄りじみた」. 「めく」 can be neutral, as in 「春めく」.

similar.title: 〜らしい (typical)
similar.explanation: 「らしい」 means having the typical qualities of the thing itself. 「めく」 means having a touch of it without really being it.

similar.title: 〜ぶる
similar.explanation: 「ぶる」 means deliberately putting on airs and is negative. 「めく」 usually describes a feeling that shows naturally.

meaning: “... goes without saying, but (even more) ...”. It acknowledges the first item and puts more weight on the second.
connection: Noun + もさることながら

senses.label: Not only ... but also
senses.meaning: First grants that the first item is obviously important or excellent, then brings up a second point that deserves even more attention. Formal. The two items are usually different aspects of the same thing.
senses.connection: Noun + もさることながら、noun + も / こそ / が ... Common: 「味もさることながら」, 「〜もさることながら、〜も大切だ」
examples: The food at this restaurant is great, of course, but the service is wonderful too.
Her singing goes without saying, and her acting is also highly praised.
Exam results matter, but the effort that leads to them matters even more.

notes: Usually used for positive evaluations, rarely for negative things.
The second item usually takes 「も」; use 「こそ」 or 「が」 for emphasis.
It follows nouns. It cannot follow a verb directly.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Telling a friend about an inn.
daily.example: The food at that inn is great, of course, but the view is the best part.

daily.title: After a movie
daily.description: Sharing impressions with a friend.
daily.example: The story was good, but the music was amazing.

work.title: Product presentation
work.description: A salesperson introduces a new product to a client.
work.example: This product excels not only in performance but also in design.

work.title: Performance review
work.description: Evaluating an employee's abilities.
work.example: His expertise goes without saying, but it's his character that earns people's trust.

etymology: 「さる」 is the attributive form of classical 「然り（さり）」, “to be so, to be natural”. 「ながら」 marks contrast. Literally: “that is true enough, but ...”.

similar.title: 〜はもとより
similar.explanation: 「はもとより」 stresses that the first item is a given, and the second is too. 「もさることながら」 puts the focus on the second.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: 「は言うまでもなく」 only says the first item goes without saying. 「もさることながら」 implies the second is more important.

similar.title: 〜はおろか
similar.explanation: 「はおろか」 usually goes with a negative: “not even ...”. 「もさることながら」 is mostly for positive evaluations.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: 「のみならず」 simply lists, “not only ... but also”. 「もさることながら」 adds a tone of evaluation and comparison.

meaning: “If only ..., but ...”. Expresses regret, dissatisfaction or reproach.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ものを (often paired with 「〜ば」 or 「〜たら」)

senses.label: If only ...
senses.meaning: At the end or in the middle of a sentence: things could have turned out better, but they didn't. It shows regret. Often 「〜ば〜たものを」.
senses.connection: 〜ば / 〜たら + verb ta-form + ものを. Common: 「〜ばよかったものを」
examples: If you'd told me sooner, I would have helped.
If only I'd been a little more careful.
If you had apologized honestly, I would have forgiven you.

senses.label: Even though ...
senses.meaning: A contrast, like 「のに」. The other person didn't do what they should have, with reproach or dissatisfaction. The second clause is usually a bad result.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + ものを、... Common: 「〜ばいいものを」
examples: You could have just kept quiet, but you said something unnecessary, and that's why you got scolded.
He should have left it alone, but he meddled again.

notes: More literary and more emotional than 「のに」.
Usually used to comment on others. About yourself, it shows regret.
In 「新しいものを買う」, 「ものを」 is just “thing + を”. It is unrelated.

daily.title: A friend gets hurt
daily.description: A friend pushed too hard and got injured, and you feel sorry.
daily.example: If only you hadn't overdone it.

daily.title: Family argument
daily.description: Blaming a family member for butting in.
daily.example: You could have just left it alone. Why did you have to interfere?

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character laments a missed chance.
daily.example: If I had just said sorry back then, we wouldn't have broken up.

work.title: A mistake at work
work.description: A coworker didn't report a problem in time, and it got worse.
work.example: If you had reported it right away, we could have dealt with it.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: Criticizing a company's slow response.
work.example: The damage could have been prevented with early measures, but the response came too late.

etymology: Formed from the formal noun 「もの」 + the particle 「を」. In classical Japanese, 「ものを」 was already a conjunctive particle of contrast (“although”) and a sentence-final particle of regret or exclamation.

similar.title: 〜のに (contrast)
similar.explanation: 「のに」 is everyday speech with wide use. 「ものを」 is more literary, with stronger regret and reproach.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: 「ばよかった」 expresses regret directly. 「ものを」 often follows 「〜ばよかった」 to strengthen the regret.

similar.title: 〜だろうに
similar.explanation: 「だろうに」 includes a guess: “it probably would have ...”. 「ものを」 is more assertive and reproachful.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「ものの」 is a plain contrast, “although ...”, with no regret or reproach.

meaning: Written style. “As soon as ...”: the second event happens right after the first.
connection: Verb dictionary form + や否や / やいなや / や

senses.label: As soon as ...
senses.meaning: Something happens almost at the same moment the first action occurs. The second event is often sudden or unexpected. Describes past facts, so the second clause is usually in the ta-form.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + や否や (やいなや)、... た
examples: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
As soon as he got home, he collapsed onto the bed.
The new product sold out as soon as it was released.

senses.label: Short form 「や」
senses.meaning: Drops 「否や」 and uses just 「や」, with the same meaning. Even more literary, usually followed by a comma.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + や、... た
examples: The moment the door opened, a child came running in.
The moment she saw my face, she burst into tears.

notes: The second clause cannot be a command, intention or request: ✕「着くや否や電話しなさい」.
Mainly used to narrate past facts. Written style.
「〜か否か」 means “whether or not”. It is a different pattern.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's hurried action.
daily.example: As soon as she read the letter, she ran out of the house.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report on how a match opened.
daily.example: No sooner had the match begun than the other team scored first.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a rush for tickets.
work.example: The tickets sold out the moment sales began.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: Describing how fast the market reacted.
work.example: As soon as the tax hike was announced, consumers started stockpiling.

etymology: 「や」 is a classical question particle, and 「否（いな）」 means “no”. 「〜や否や」 is thought to have originally meant “before it is clear whether ... or not”: the next thing happens before you can tell if the first is finished. Hence “as soon as”.

similar.title: 〜が早いか
similar.explanation: Very close in meaning, and both are written style. 「が早いか」 stresses that the second action happens the instant the first ends, usually by the same person.

similar.title: 〜なり (as soon as)
similar.explanation: With 「なり」, both clauses must have the same subject, and it usually describes an unexpected action. With 「や否や」, the subjects can differ.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「たとたん」 follows the ta-form and is common in everyday speech. 「や否や」 follows the dictionary form and is written style.

similar.title: 〜次第 (as soon as)
similar.explanation: 「次第」 is for future events, and the second clause can be a request or intention. 「や否や」 only narrates things that already happened.

meaning: Written style. Expresses cause, “because of ...”. At the start of a sentence, 「ゆえに」 means “therefore”.
connection: Noun (の) / na-adjective (である) / plain form + ゆえ（に）/ ゆえの + noun; often 「〜がゆえに」

senses.label: Because of ...
senses.meaning: Gives a cause or reason. Stiff and formal, found in writing and speeches. 「〜がゆえに」 is stronger.
senses.connection: Noun + ゆえ（に）; plain form / noun + である + がゆえに
examples: Because of poverty, he couldn't go to school.
Precisely because he is honest, he often loses out.
Given the circumstances, we ask for your understanding.

senses.label: ... that comes from ...
senses.meaning: 「ゆえの + noun」 means “... that arises because of ...”. A typical phrase is 「若さゆえの過ち」.
senses.connection: Noun + ゆえの + noun; 〜がゆえの + noun
examples: That was a mistake of youth.
There are worries that come precisely from being a parent.

senses.label: Therefore (sentence-initial)
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, it works as a conjunction like 「だから」 or 「したがって」. Used in logical reasoning such as math proofs and academic papers.
senses.connection: Start of sentence + ゆえに (故に)、...
examples: A equals B, and B equals C. Therefore, A equals C.
I think, therefore I am.

notes: It's written style. In everyday conversation, 「から」 or 「ので」 is enough.
It can be written with the kanji 「故」, but the 「故」 in 「事故」 or 「故障」 is unrelated.
「それゆえ」 means “therefore” and works like sentence-initial 「ゆえに」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character looks back on the past.
daily.example: With the recklessness of youth, I ran away from home without thinking.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: The narrator explains how an animal survives.
daily.example: Precisely because they are small, they protect themselves in groups.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Drawing a conclusion in an argument.
work.example: The experimental results above support the hypothesis. Therefore, the aim of this study can be said to have been achieved.

work.title: Formal greeting
work.description: Explaining a reason in a formal message.
work.example: As I am still new to this, I may cause you some inconvenience, but I look forward to working with you.

etymology: 「ゆえ」 is written 「故」 and originally means “reason, cause”. Classical Japanese often used 「〜ゆえに」 for causes, and it survives today in written language.

similar.title: 〜から (cause/reason)
similar.explanation: 「から」 is everyday language. 「ゆえに」 is stiff written style with a flavor of logical reasoning.

similar.title: 〜ために
similar.explanation: 「ために」 can also show cause and is used in both speech and writing. 「ゆえに」 is more classical and formal.

similar.title: 〜ばかりに
similar.explanation: 「ばかりに」 means “just because ... (something bad happened)”, with regret. 「ゆえに」 is a neutral statement of cause.

similar.title: 〜だけに
similar.explanation: 「だけに」 means “precisely because ..., all the more ...”, stressing degree. 「ゆえに」 only shows cause and effect.

meaning: “Apart from ..., there is no (other) ...”. Praises someone or something as the only suitable choice.
connection: Noun + をおいて (ほかに) ... ない

senses.label: No one / nothing but ...
senses.meaning: There is no other suitable person or thing. It expresses high praise. Always paired with a negative.
senses.connection: Noun + をおいて (ほかに / 他に) ... ない / いない
examples: He is the only one we can entrust with this job.
If you want to learn traditional Japanese culture, there's no place like Kyoto.
Ms. Tanaka is probably the only person fit to be the next president.

senses.label: Above all else
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「何をおいても」 means “putting everything else aside, first ...”. It stresses priority.
senses.connection: 何をおいても + expression of will or obligation
examples: When an earthquake hits, you should first and foremost make sure you are safe.
When I heard my mother had collapsed, I dropped everything and rushed to her.

notes: Only for positive evaluations. You can't say ✕「彼をおいて悪い人はいない」.
In 「荷物を置いて出かける」, 「置いて」 means “to leave something”. It is unrelated.
Usually written in kana: 「おいて」.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Telling a friend where to see cherry blossoms.
daily.example: For cherry blossoms, nothing beats Yoshino.

daily.title: A friend needs help
daily.description: A friend is in trouble, and you decide to help first.
daily.example: If a friend is in trouble, I'll drop everything and go help.

work.title: Proposing a leader
work.description: Recommending a project leader at a meeting.
work.example: I can't think of anyone but Mr. Yamamoto to lead this project.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting on an athlete's ability.
work.example: He is probably the one and only favorite to win this tournament.

etymology: The verb 「おく（置く）」 can mean “to set aside, to exclude”. 「〜をおいて」 literally means “if you set ... aside (there is nothing else)”.

similar.title: 〜を除いて
similar.explanation: 「を除いて」 objectively means “except for ...”. 「をおいて」 carries high praise, “only ... will do”, and is followed by a negative.

similar.title: 〜に限る
similar.explanation: 「に限る」 means “... is best”. 「をおいて〜ない」 means “there is nothing but ...”, a stronger evaluation.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: 「にほかならない」 means “is nothing other than ...” and pins down a cause or essence. 「をおいて」 stresses the one and only choice.

meaning: Marks a point in time as the last; after it, something stops. Also used in 「声を限りに」, “at the top of one's voice”.
connection: Noun (今日, 本日, 今回, etc.) + を限りに

senses.label: As of ... (last time)
senses.meaning: Something that has been going on ends at this point in time. Used to announce quitting, retiring or closing. The second clause is usually about ending or stopping.
senses.connection: Time noun (今日, 本日, 今回, 今年度, etc.) + を限りに
examples: As of today, I'm quitting smoking.
Our store will close its doors after today.
She will retire at the end of this season.

senses.label: With all one's might
senses.meaning: The set phrase 「声を限りに」 means shouting as loudly as possible. It is a fixed expression.
senses.connection: 声 + を限りに + 叫ぶ, 呼ぶ, etc.
examples: He cried for help at the top of his voice.
The spectators cheered the players at the top of their lungs.

notes: It usually follows time nouns meaning “now”, like 「今日」, 「本日」 or 「今回」.
More formal than 「〜を最後に」.
In 「先着百名に限り」, 「に限り」 means “limited to”. It is a different pattern.

daily.title: Making a resolution
daily.description: Telling your family you'll break a bad habit.
daily.example: Starting today, no more staying up late!

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report that a famous athlete is retiring.
daily.example: I heard that player is retiring after this tournament.

work.title: Closing notice
work.description: A notice posted by a shop that is closing.
work.example: We regret to inform you that we will cease business as of today.

work.title: Farewell speech
work.description: Saying goodbye to coworkers at a farewell party.
work.example: I will be leaving the company at the end of this month. Thank you for everything.

etymology: 「限り」 is the noun form of the verb 「限る」, meaning “limit, boundary”. 「〜を限りに」 means “taking ... as the limit”, hence “with ... as the last”.

similar.title: 〜をもって (deadline)
similar.explanation: 「をもって」 usually marks deadlines in formal notices. 「を限りに」 stresses “this is the end; no more after this”.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: 「を境に」 marks a dividing line in time, with a change before and after. 「を限りに」 means something ends there.

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: 「を機に」 means taking an event as a chance to start something new. 「を限りに」 focuses on ending.

similar.title: 〜に限り
similar.explanation: 「に限り」 means “only, limited to” and restricts scope. 「を限りに」 marks the final point in time.

meaning: Starting with one event, similar events follow one after another.
connection: Noun + を皮切りに (して) / を皮切りとして

senses.label: Starting with ...
senses.meaning: Something is the first of a series of actions or events. The second clause usually means “one after another, in succession, spreading”. Common with events, tours and business expansion.
senses.connection: Noun + を皮切りに (して)、... (次々と, 相次いで, 全国で, etc.); noun + を皮切りとして
examples: Kicking off with the Tokyo show, the nationwide tour is about to begin.
Starting with his comment, objections came one after another.
Starting with this store, we plan to open ten stores overseas.

notes: The second clause usually describes a series of similar events, not just a single one.
It isn't used for the speaker's everyday personal matters. Common in news and business.
「皮切り」 can also be used alone as a noun, as in 「〜が皮切りとなった」.

daily.title: Following an idol
daily.description: Fans talk about their idol's tour schedule.
daily.example: I heard the Asia tour kicks off with the Osaka show next month.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on a chain of events.
daily.example: Starting with one accusation, similar reports of harm followed one after another.

work.title: Business plan
work.description: A company announces its overseas expansion.
work.example: Starting with our Shanghai store, we will expand across Asia.

work.title: Event planning
work.description: Explaining the schedule of a series of events.
work.example: Starting with the April seminar, we will hold training sessions throughout the year.

etymology: 「皮切り」 originally meant the very first burn in moxibustion. That first burn on the skin hurts the most, so it was called “cutting the skin”. Later it came to mean “the very beginning” of something.

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: 「をはじめ」 gives a representative example: “... and others, led by ...”. 「を皮切りに」 is about time: “starting with ...”.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: 「をきっかけに」 means an event triggered a change. 「を皮切りに」 marks the first of a series of similar events.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: 「を契機に」 is the written version of 「をきっかけに」, focusing on the trigger. 「を皮切りに」 focuses on a continuing series.

meaning: Written style. One cannot help feeling a certain emotion about something.
connection: Noun (同情, 怒り, 驚き, 涙, 憤り, etc.) + を禁じ得ない

senses.label: Cannot help feeling ...
senses.meaning: After seeing or hearing something, a strong emotion wells up naturally and can't be held back. It follows emotion nouns. Formal, used in writing or official statements.
senses.connection: Emotion noun + を禁じ得ない / を禁じ得なかった / を禁じ得ません
examples: Hearing the disaster victims' stories, I couldn't help feeling sympathy for them.
I can't help feeling angry at such an unfair ruling.
I cannot help being astonished at the truth behind that incident.

notes: It only follows emotion nouns, not verbs.
It is not used for the speaker's own actions, but for reactions to outside events.
In speech, say 「〜ずにはいられない」 or 「つい〜てしまう」.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: Reading a report about an outrageous crime.
daily.example: I can't help feeling indignant at crimes that target the vulnerable.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: Moved by a touching documentary.
daily.example: The way he lived his life brought me to tears.

work.title: Official statement
work.description: A company issues a statement about an accident.
work.example: We deeply regret this accident.

work.title: Book review
work.description: A critic reviews a work.
work.example: One cannot help but marvel at the depth of the author's insight.

etymology: 「禁じる」 means “to forbid, to suppress”, and 「得ない」 means “cannot”. Literally: “cannot suppress (this feeling)”.

similar.title: 〜ないではいられない
similar.explanation: 「ないではいられない」 follows verbs and works in speech and writing. 「を禁じ得ない」 follows emotion nouns and is stiff written style.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: 「てならない」 expresses a feeling that stays strong. 「を禁じ得ない」 expresses an emotion that wells up in response to something outside.

similar.title: 〜てやまない
similar.explanation: 「てやまない」 means continually holding a feeling (hope, respect, etc.), usually positive. 「を禁じ得ない」 is usually sympathy, anger, and the like.

similar.title: 〜に堪えない
similar.explanation: 「に堪えない」 can also express strong emotion, as in 「感謝に堪えない」 (“deeply grateful”). Often used in formal speeches.

meaning: Written style. Marks means or method, “with, by means of ...”; also a time limit, “as of ... (ending)”.
connection: Noun + をもって / をもちまして (more polite)

senses.label: By means of ...
senses.meaning: The means, method or attitude used to do something. Like 「で」, but formal. Common in official notices and writing.
senses.connection: Noun (書面, 誠意, 拍手, etc.) + をもって. Common: 「書面をもって」, 「誠意をもって」, 「身をもって」
examples: We will notify you of the results in writing.
He apologized sincerely.
The athletes were welcomed with warm applause.

senses.label: As of ... (deadline)
senses.meaning: Something ends at this point in time. Used to formally announce an end or a deadline. The politer form is 「をもちまして」.
senses.connection: Time noun (本日, 今月末, 〇月〇日, etc.) + をもって / をもちまして + ending, closing, leaving, etc.
examples: We will be closing our business as of today.
I will be leaving the company as of March 31.
This concludes the meeting.

senses.label: As the standard
senses.meaning: Marks the standard or basis for a decision. Common in rules and regulations.
senses.connection: Noun + をもって + 〜とする
examples: A score of 60 or higher counts as a pass.
Confirmation of attendance will serve as registration.

notes: Written style. In everyday conversation, 「で」 is usually used.
「をもちまして」 is even more polite, common in speeches and announcements.
「をもってすれば / をもってしても」 is a separate pattern: “with ..., (one can) / even with ...”.
「持って」 meaning “holding”, as in 「傘を持って」, is unrelated.

daily.title: Store announcement
daily.description: An announcement before a shopping mall closes.
daily.example: Today's business hours will end at 8 p.m.

daily.title: Sharing an experience
daily.description: Telling a friend about something you learned firsthand.
daily.example: I learned firsthand how important health is.

work.title: Official notice
work.description: HR informs applicants of the results.
work.example: We will inform you in writing at a later date whether you have been hired.

work.title: Chairing a meeting
work.description: The chair announces the end of the meeting.
work.example: With that, we will conclude today's meeting.

work.title: Farewell email
work.description: An employee sends a goodbye email to everyone.
work.example: I will be leaving the company at the end of September.

etymology: 「もって」 is a sound-changed form of 「持ちて」. In kanbun reading it was used to read the character 「以」, so it took on the meaning “by means of”. It is often written 「以て」.

similar.title: 〜で (means/method)
similar.explanation: 「で」 is the ordinary form. 「をもって」 means the same but is formal and written.

similar.title: 〜を限りに
similar.explanation: Both can mark a deadline. 「を限りに」 stresses “this is the end; no more after this”. 「をもって」 is common in formal announcements.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「によって」 marks means, cause, basis and more, with wider use. 「をもって」 leans toward means and deadlines in formal settings.

similar.title: 〜をもってすれば
similar.explanation: 「をもってすれば」 means “with ..., (one can surely) ...”, stressing great ability. It differs from plain 「をもって」.
